subtopics.title: Madhya Pradesh High Court Judgment
subtopics.summary: The Madhya Pradesh High Court declared the Bhojshala - Kamal Maula Complex a Hindu temple and quashed the 2003 ASI order that allowed shared worship. It held that the Places of Worship Act, 1991 did not apply because the site is a protected monument. The court also directed the State Government to consider alternative land in Dhar for a mosque or prayer site.
facts: The MP High Court declared the complex a Hindu temple of Goddess Vagdevi (Saraswati), based on 2024 ASI survey findings.
The court quashed the 2003 ASI order that had allowed shared worship at the site.
The Places of Worship Act, 1991 was held inapplicable because the site falls under the AMASR Act, 1958 as a protected monument.
Section 4(3) of the Places of Worship Act excludes ancient monuments under the AMASR Act, 1958 from the religious character freeze.
The Muslim side's reliance on an August 1935 proclamation by the princely State of Dhar was rejected.
The Government of India Act, 1935 was not enforced until April 1937.
The case was treated as a Writ Petition under Article 226 seeking enforcement of the fundamental right to worship.
Unlike the Babri Masjid dispute (a Title Suit over ownership), the Bhojshala case was a writ petition.
The State Government was directed to consider allotting alternative land within Dhar for a mosque or prayer site.

subtopics.title: Places of Worship Act, 1991
subtopics.summary: The Places of Worship Act, 1991 freezes the religious character of places of worship as it stood on 15 August 1947 and prohibits their conversion. It terminates pre-1947 disputes, allows new cases only for post-1947 changes, and provides penalties for violations. The Act has drawn criticism on grounds of judicial review, federalism, equality and the 1947 cut-off date.
facts: The Act was passed by the P V Narasimha Rao-led Congress government.
Section 3 prohibits converting a place of worship between or within religious denominations.
Section 4(1) ensures the religious identity of a place of worship remains as it was on August 15, 1947.
Section 4(2) terminates legal proceedings on pre-1947 religious character conversions; new cases are allowed only for post-1947 changes.
Section 5 provides exceptions for ancient monuments under the AMASR Act, 1958 and for the Ayodhya dispute.
Section 6 provides penalties with a maximum imprisonment term of 3 years, along with fines.
Critics say the Act bars judicial review, limiting constitutional checks and balances.
Critics say the Act violates the right to religion (Art 25-28) and undermines equality (Art 14-15).
Critics say the August 15, 1947 cut-off ignores historical injustices and pre-1947 encroachments.
The Supreme Court's 2019 Ayodhya verdict said the Act upholds secular values and prohibits retrogression.

subtopics.title: Historical and Religious Claims
subtopics.summary: The site is a medieval ASI-protected monument in Dhar, Madhya Pradesh, traditionally linked to Raja Bhoj, who built it in 1034 AD. Hindus regard it as a Saraswati temple, while Muslims identify it as the Kamal Maula Mosque. It was reportedly converted into a mosque in 1514 AD, and an idol of Goddess Saraswati found at the site is now in the British Museum, London.
facts: Medieval ASI-protected monument located in Dhar, Madhya Pradesh.
Hindus claim the site as a Saraswati temple; Muslims consider it a mosque.
Built by Raja Bhoj in 1034 AD.
The term 'Bhojshala' became linked to the building in the early 20th century, based on inscriptions found at the site by KK Lele.
The structure is believed to have originally functioned as a temple dedicated to Goddess Saraswati (Vagdevi).
Reportedly converted into a mosque in 1514 AD under Muslim rule (Mehmudshah Khilji) in Dhar.
Muslims identify the structure as the Kamal Maula Mosque, associated with Sufi saint Hazrat Maulana Kamaluddin Chishti.
An intricately carved idol of Goddess Saraswati was discovered at the site during excavations in the 20th century.
The Saraswati idol is currently housed in the British Museum, London.
The site was traditionally regarded as a centre of Sanskrit learning and scholarship.

subtopics.title: Architecture, Inscriptions and Gurjara-Pratihara Links
subtopics.summary: The complex preserves the remains of a Mandapa-style hall, typical of Hindu temple architecture, and two Sarpabandha pillar inscriptions that teach Sanskrit grammar. Its walls carry odes to Kurma Avatara in Prakrit, and its inscriptions mention Paramara rulers. Raja Bhoj, recognized as Mihir Bhoja, is linked to the Gurjara-Pratihara Empire.
facts: Structural remains indicate a Mandapa-style hall, characteristic of Hindu temple architecture.
The site uniquely preserves 2 Sarpabandha (serpentine chart) pillar inscriptions.
The Sarpabandha inscriptions chart the Sanskrit alphabet, noun/verb terminations, and the ten tenses and moods of Sanskrit grammar.
Stone slabs on the walls carry two odes to Kurma Avatara (Tortoise Incarnation of Vishnu), composed in Prakrit.
Sanskrit and Pali inscriptions mention Paramara rulers such as Udayaditya, Naravarman and Arjunavarma Deva.
The Sanskrit drama Karpuramanjari was written by royal tutor Madana, a disciple of Jain scholar Ashadhara.
Gurjara-Pratihara Empire founder: Nagabhata I (730-756 AD).
Raja Bhoj (Mihir Bhoja) was the most illustrious emperor of the Gurjara-Pratihara Empire.
Capital of the Gurjara-Pratihara Empire: Kannauj (Mahodaya).
The Pratiharas were central to a tripartite struggle against the Palas of Bengal and the Rashtrakutas of the Deccan.

quizzes.passage: The Madhya Pradesh High Court has ruled on the Bhojshala - Kamal Maula Complex, a medieval monument in Dhar, Madhya Pradesh. Relying on findings from a survey by the Archaeological Survey of India, the court declared the complex a Hindu temple dedicated to Goddess Vagdevi, another name for Saraswati. In the same ruling, the court quashed an earlier ASI order that had allowed shared worship at the site. The bench held that the Places of Worship Act, 1991 could not be applied here, because the site is a protected monument under the Ancient Monuments and Archaeological Sites and Remains Act, 1958. The freeze on religious character in the Act does not extend to such monuments. The Muslim side had relied on a proclamation issued by the princely State of Dhar in 1935. The bench rejected this reliance, noting that the Government of India Act, 1935, on which the proclamation rested, had not been enforced until a later date. The case was treated as a writ petition seeking enforcement of the fundamental right to worship, unlike the Babri Masjid dispute, which was a title suit about ownership. To balance the rights of both communities, the court directed the State Government to consider applications for allotting alternative land within Dhar for a mosque or prayer site.

quizzes.passage: The Places of Worship Act, 1991 was passed by a Congress government to protect the religious identity of places of worship. Its central aim is to keep the religious character of each place as it stood on Independence Day. The Act prohibits converting a place of worship from one religious denomination to another, whether between or within denominations. It terminates pending legal proceedings about religious character conversions that took place before the cut-off, while allowing new cases about changes made after it. Violating the Act attracts imprisonment and fines. The Act exempts ancient monuments protected under the Ancient Monuments and Archaeological Sites and Remains Act, and it does not cover the Ayodhya dispute and related legal proceedings. Critics argue that the Act limits judicial review, weakening constitutional checks and balances. Others say that it violates the right to freedom of religion and treats communities differently, undermining equality. Critics also argue that the Independence Day cut-off ignores historical injustices and earlier encroachments. The Supreme Court, in its verdict on the Ayodhya dispute, said that the Act upholds secular values and prohibits retrogression. Its supporters say the Act ensures the preservation of religious sites and their character, instilling confidence in all communities. Together, these points explain why the Act remains a contested law.
